question: What identifying number must be added by labeling to a batch as soon as it is certified?

review.note: (a) certified lot number; 70.25(d) partial; overlaps 80.38-1

question: How long do we have to keep track of where every pound of an approved dye lot went?

review.note: until at least 2 years after disposal

question: We received a certificate for a 500-lb batch of FD&C Yellow No. 6, used 200 lb in our own soaps and sold the rest to three customers. What must our logs show?
Under Part 80, may we keep our certified-color shipment logs inside our general ERP records, or must they be separate?

review.note: (c) kept separately

question: Must FDA staff be allowed to inventory our stock of a certified color to check our distribution records?

review.note: (a) inventory; 80.34(a)(3) gives the consequence only

question: Are FD&C lakes only approved on a temporary basis, or do they have a permanent approval?

review.note: (a) FD&C lakes provisionally listed until closing dates; 82.51 only implies it via the Part title

question: We want to use a D&C lake that is provisionally listed for drugs and cosmetics in a liquid eyeliner. Is eye-area use allowed?

review.note: 81.1 bars eye-area use explicitly; 70.5(a) general rule gives the same result

question: Under Part 81, for which product uses are Ext. D&C lakes provisionally listed?

review.note: (c) externally applied drugs/cosmetics; writer's alt 82.2051 states use only via subpart title (partial); corpus 81.1 cross-refs are garbled ((b) D&C lakes->82.2051, (c)->'82.105(1)')

question: Do companies relying on a provisionally listed color have to send FDA progress reports, and how often?

review.note: by Jan 1 1968, then every 6 months, unless a petition was filed

question: Why is graphite no longer allowed as a colorant in skin-applied cosmetics, and from what date did FDA end its interim acceptance?

review.note: (j) gives PNA contamination reason and Nov 29, 1977 date; graphite appears nowhere else (81.30 has no graphite certificate paragraph).

question: A contract manufacturer wants to revive a 1970s lipstick shade built on D&C Red No. 10 and D&C Red No. 12. Can those colors still be used, and why were they dropped?

review.note: (h) gives termination plus why (petition withdrawn, beta-naphthylamine). Writer's 81.30 is only partial: (k)(1) cancels certificates/adulteration but has no reason, so it is not equal.

question: What did the rat, mouse and dog feeding studies show that led FDA to end the interim listing of FD&C Red No. 1?

review.note: (c)(1)-(3) give rat/mouse/dog liver findings; 81.30(b) only cancels certificates.

question: Under Part 81, is FD&C Red No. 4 still provisionally allowed in food or ingested drugs, and which external uses remain listed for it?

review.note: (d)(3) answers both halves. 81.30(c) (also Part 81) says certificates are void for food/ingested drugs/ingested cosmetics but continue for externally applied drugs and cosmetics, so it is equal. 74.2304 (external cosmetics only) and 82.304 (outside Part 81) are partial.

question: Does an old FDA batch approval for FD&C Red No. 2 still let anyone use that dye in food or cosmetics today?

review.note: (j)(1): certificates void after Jan 28, 1976; use = adulteration. Writer's 81.10(f) only ends the listing and says nothing on the old batch certificates (partial, not equal).

question: A lip-gloss maker still has tubes, filled in early 1988, colored with a D&C Red No. 9 lake. After the July 1988 cutoff, did FDA require those finished tubes off the market?

review.note: (s)(3)-(4): cutoff July 15, 1988; no removal required for lip products colored on/before that date. The framing is historical (tubes from 1988 'still' held), but the question is answerable.

question: After FDA voided D&C Blue No. 6 certificates for drugs and cosmetics, could batches of that color still be certified for coloring surgical sutures?

review.note: (o)(1) says D&C Blue No. 6 continues to be certified for surgical sutures. 74.3106(c)/(e) lists it for sutures, with batches certified under Part 80.

question: From what date did certificates for FD&C Red No. 3 lakes and D&C Red No. 3 lakes stop having any effect for cosmetics, and what follows if they're used afterward?

review.note: (u)(1) covers FD&C and D&C Red No. 3 lakes, Jan 29, 1990, and adulteration. Writer's 81.10(u) omits D&C Red No. 3 lakes and the consequence (partial).

question: In the older coal-tar color rules, what exactly are alumina and blanc fixe when they're mentioned as bases for lakes?

review.note: (g)/(h) define both terms. 82.1051/82.2051 name them as substrata but do not define them. 73.1010 alumina is a different (dried) color additive.

question: Our lab's assay report for a provisionally listed coal-tar color gives a 'mixed oxides' figure. Which metals go into that number, and as what compounds are they calculated?

review.note: (j) is the only 'mixed oxides' text in the corpus.

question: Under Part 82, would a tinted lip balm or a product used on mucous membranes count as 'externally applied' for colors limited to external use?

review.note: (n) excludes lips/mucous membranes. 70.3(v) has an identical definition, though the question's 'Under Part 82' points to 82.3.

question: Where the provisional coal-tar color specifications use words such as 'cosmetic' or 'label' without explaining them, what meaning applies?

review.note: (q) applies FD&C Act 201 meanings. 700.3(n)/700.27(a) have similar clauses but for other parts, not the coal-tar specifications.

question: How much lead and arsenic may a batch of an FD&C dye on FDA's interim color list contain and still get certified?

review.note: (b)(1)(i)-(ii) give Pb 0.001% and As2O3 0.00014%. Color-specific Part 82 sections only cross-refer to Part 74 specs; the generic question fits 82.5.

question: Under Part 82, we're submitting a batch of a barium-salt D&C pigment for lipsticks for certification. What's the ceiling on soluble barium?

review.note: (b)(3) soluble barium <=0.05% as BaCl2 is the only soluble-barium text.

question: Are the heavy-metal limits for a provisionally listed D&C or Ext. D&C color looser than those for an FD&C color, and by how much?

review.note: Comparing (b)(1) and (b)(2): lead is double, arsenic and heavy metals are looser.

question: Besides the numeric metal limits, must a coal-tar color batch on the interim list be free of avoidable impurities before FDA will certify it?

review.note: (a) requires freedom from impurities avoidable by GMP. Similar clauses in Part 73/74 are color-specific, not the interim list.

question: If an FD&C color on FDA's interim list passes certification, can that one lot be used in foods, medicines and makeup alike?

review.note: 82.50 says a subpart B batch is certifiable for food, drugs and cosmetics. 81.1(a) lists only FD&C lakes, so it is partial here, though its eye-area exclusion is relevant to 'makeup'.

question: A confectioner and a mouthwash brand want to split one certified lot of FD&C Blue No. 2 bought under the provisionally listed color rules. Is that lot good for both?

review.note: By text, 82.50 says yes to both uses. Caveat: the straight FD&C Blue No. 2 is permanently listed only for food (74.102), ingested drugs (74.1102) and devices, not cosmetics, and 81.1(a) provisionally lists only lakes. The 'provisional' premise is vestigial; the answer to the mouthwash half may mislead in the answer stage.

question: What standards does a batch of a provisional food-drug-cosmetic color have to meet before FDA certifies it for all three uses?

review.note: 82.50 only points to 82.5 plus the color's own specs; 82.5 holds the actual standards. needs_also 82.5 is listed.

question: Which kinds of products can a certified FD&C aluminum lake from the interim color list go into?

review.note: The question is about FD&C lakes. 81.1(a) directly lists Lakes (FD&C) for food, drug and cosmetic use and adds the eye-area and suture exclusions. 82.50 covers straight colors and reaches lakes only through 82.51(b). Keep 82.50+82.51 as supporting.

question: Is a certified lot of a D&C color on FDA's interim list usable in candy or other foods, or just medicines and cosmetics?

review.note: 'for use only in drugs and cosmetics' answers it directly; 81.1(b) covers D&C lakes only.

question: Our mouthwash uses a certified lot of D&C Yellow No. 10 from the provisional list; a sister company wants the same lot for gummy bears. Can the food use go ahead?

review.note: 'only in drugs and cosmetics' means no food use. 82.1710 only cross-refers to 74.1710 specs.

question: Before FDA certifies a batch of a straight color from the provisional drug-and-cosmetic group, what requirements must it conform to?

review.note: 82.1050 points to 82.5 plus subpart C specs; 82.5 holds the requirements. needs_also 82.5 is listed.

question: Food makers ask whether a certified D&C lake from the interim drug-and-cosmetic group is open to them, or limited to drugs and cosmetics. Which is it?

review.note: The 'only' in 82.1050 answers it once 82.1051(b) makes the lake a subpart C straight color (needs_also listed). 81.1(b) lists Lakes (D&C) for drug and cosmetic use directly.

question: Could a certified lot of an Ext. D&C color from FDA's interim list go into a lipstick, or only into products put on the outer skin?

review.note: 82.2050 limits use to externally applied products; the lipstick exclusion needs 82.3(n) (listed) or the identical 70.3(v).

question: We're certifying a batch of Ext. D&C Yellow No. 7 under Part 82 for both a body lotion and a lip gloss. Which product may use it?

review.note: 82.2707a states this color is restricted to externally applied drugs and cosmetics. Both need 82.3(n) to rule out lip gloss. 74.2707a is outside the named Part 82.

question: For a provisional color restricted to externally applied products, what must each batch conform to before it can be certified?

review.note: 82.2050 points to 82.5 plus subpart D specs; needs_also 82.5 is listed.

question: Are certified Ext. D&C lakes on the interim list allowed in externally applied drugs as well as cosmetics?

review.note: 82.2050 covers straight colors; lakes come in through 82.2051(b) (needs_also listed). 81.1(c) lists Lakes (Ext. D&C) for externally applied drugs and cosmetics directly.

question: If one of our products sells only about $800 a year, does FDA consider it sold commercially for purposes of its voluntary cosmetic programs?

review.note: (i) sets commercial distribution at annual gross sales over $1,000. The $1,000,000 in FD&C 612 is an unrelated threshold.

question: We handed out 3,000 free samples of a new serum, about $1,500 in cost of goods, and ran a two-city test market. Does that count as distributing it outside our plant?

review.note: (o): free samples/market testing over $1,000 in cost of goods. Read literally, 'count as distributing it outside our plant' is trivially yes; the intent is the commercial-distribution definition.

question: A customer says our lotion gave her a rash. What makes that a 'reportable experience', and can a screening procedure on file with FDA rule it out?

review.note: (q) reportable experience and (p) filed screening procedure. FD&C 604(5) serious adverse event is a different concept.

question: Is a contract filler that only relabels and swaps bottles doing 'packaging' of a cosmetic, as FDA's cosmetic regulations use that word?

review.note: (l): labeling or changing the immediate container is packaging. FD&C 604(3)(C) defines packaging only for facility exclusions (statute, not 'regulations').

question: Which antibacterial, once used in deodorant bars and blemish cover creams, did FDA rule makes a cosmetic adulterated because it causes lasting light sensitivity?

review.note: (a) names detergent bars and blemish bases, plus persistent photosensitivity. 700.15 (salicylanilides) is a near-competitor, also with persistent photosensitization, but it names no bar or blemish products and covers four agents.

question: An importer in Miami has a shipment of shampoo bars whose ingredient list shows bithionol as the antibacterial. Can those bars be sold as cosmetics?

review.note: Under (a), any bithionol cosmetic is adulterated; FD&C 601/301 are only generic.

question: For cosmetics containing bithionol, after what shipment date could FDA begin regulatory proceedings?

review.note: (b) March 15, 1968. The question repeats the 3-word heading 'cosmetics containing bithionol', but only 'bithionol' is distinctive and it is needed to name the substance. Not counted as a leak; borderline.

question: Is there any acceptable amount of bithionol in a cosmetic, or does any amount make the product adulterated?

review.note: (a): 'any cosmetic containing bithionol' is adulterated, with no threshold.

question: Can a fade cream for freckles and age spots legally use an Hg-based active and still be sold as a beauty product?

review.note: (d)(1) says mercury skin-bleaching products sold as beauty preparations are misbranded and may be unapproved new drugs.

question: A mascara maker preserves its formula with thimerosal at 50 ppm mercury because no other preservative controls Pseudomonas in it. Is that permitted?

review.note: (d)(2)(ii): eye-area only, <=65 ppm, no safe nonmercurial substitute, so 50 ppm is permitted.

question: What trace level of mercury can a face lotion contain without being adulterated, if the trace is unavoidable under good manufacturing practice?

review.note: (d)(2)(i): unavoidable trace below 1 ppm.

question: Under Part 700, may mercury compounds still serve as preservatives in hand creams and shampoos, given that safer substitutes exist?

review.note: (c)-(d) say no, except eye-area cosmetics.

question: A private-label supplier offers a cheap dry-shampoo spray whose propellant blend includes vinyl chloride. If we ship it to retailers in other states, what's our exposure?

review.note: (a) adulterated and (b) subject to regulatory action when shipped. FD&C 301 is only a generic basis.

question: Is every cosmetic aerosol shipped interstate with vinyl chloride as an ingredient subject to FDA regulatory action, regardless of the amount?

review.note: (b) covers any such aerosol; no threshold is stated, which implies 'regardless of amount'. Repeats 'vinyl chloride as an ingredient' from the heading, but only the substance name is distinctive. Borderline, not counted as a leak.

question: Does the vinyl chloride ban cover only hair sprays, or any cosmetic aerosol that contains it as an ingredient?

review.note: (a) applies to 'any cosmetic aerosol product', not only hair sprays.

question: Why did FDA ban the brominated antimicrobials TBS, DBS and MBS from cosmetics, and what harm do they cause?

review.note: (a)-(b): photosensitizers and cross-sensitizers causing disabling skin disorders.

question: Our startup bought a 1974 deodorant bar formula that uses 3,3',4,5'-tetrachlorosalicylanilide at 0.5%. If we relaunch it next spring, what happens?

review.note: TCSA is adulterated at any level under (b); (c) gives regulatory action after Dec 1, 1975.

question: For cosmetics containing tribromsalan, does FDA's enforcement cutoff turn on the manufacturing date or the date first shipped interstate, and what is that date?

review.note: (c): initial interstate introduction after Dec 1, 1975.

question: Is any level of these salicylanilide antimicrobials allowed in a cosmetic for any purpose, or is it an outright ban?

review.note: (b) 'at any level for any purpose'. 'these' has no antecedent, but 'salicylanilide antimicrobials' still identifies the class.

question: What health problem led FDA to treat spray-can antiperspirants with Zr complexes as unsafe for users?

review.note: (a): lung granulomas; 'Zr' is a plausible chemist's shorthand.

question: Our contract maker wants to turn our aluminum zirconium stick deodorant into an aerosol spray for a 2027 launch. Is there a regulatory obstacle?

review.note: (b): any aerosol cosmetic containing zirconium is adulterated.

question: When did FDA start taking action against zirconium-containing aerosol cosmetics introduced into interstate commerce?

review.note: (c): after Sept 15, 1977.

question: Does the zirconium restriction reach non-aerosol forms like sticks and creams, or only sprays that can reach the lungs?

review.note: (a)-(b) are limited to aerosol form; nothing in the corpus covers non-aerosol zirconium.

question: Why can't cosmetics include trichloromethane as an ingredient, and what did the cancer studies show?

review.note: (a): NCI liver/renal tumors; trichloromethane is a real synonym.

question: A European partner's nail-polish remover formula contains chloroform at 2% as a solvent. Can we sell it in the US as a cosmetic?

review.note: (b): 2% as a formula solvent is an ingredient, not a residual processing solvent, so it is adulterated.

question: Does chloroform left over only from its use as a processing solvent, or as a byproduct of making an ingredient, count against our lotion?

review.note: (b): residual processing-solvent or byproduct chloroform is not treated as an ingredient.

question: Is a cosmetic with chloroform as an intentional ingredient adulterated regardless of level, and is it subject to regulatory action?

review.note: (b): adulterated and subject to action under 301/601(a).

question: Can a hair spray use dichloromethane as a solvent at around 15 percent of the formula?

review.note: (a)-(b); dichloromethane is a standard synonym.

question: A salon hairspray imported from overseas lists DCM at 20%. If our distribution company brings it in and sells it, what is FDA's position?

review.note: (b) says adulterated and subject to action; DCM is a common abbreviation.

question: Is a cosmetic adulterated just because methylene chloride is one of its ingredients, even if it isn't an aerosol hair spray?

review.note: (b) applies to 'any cosmetic product', not only aerosol hair sprays.

question: What National Toxicology Program finding led FDA to conclude that methylene chloride in cosmetics poses a significant cancer risk?

review.note: (a): NTP 2-year inhalation study, lung/liver tumors in mice.

question: Can our body mist still use the old ozone-depleting spray gases to push the product out of the can?

review.note: 700.23 prohibits CFC propellants (via 2.125, not in the corpus). 740.11(c) matches 'ozone-depleting' lexically but covers only labeling (40 CFR 82), so it is a distractor, not an alternative.

question: An overseas factory quotes a lower price on a dry-shampoo can filled with CFC-11 and CFC-12. Can we import and sell it?

review.note: CFC-11/12 propellant is prohibited.

question: Does FDA's ban on chlorofluorocarbons cover self-pressurized cosmetic containers, and is the actual prohibition set out in the cosmetic rules or in a general FDA rule?

review.note: Covers self-pressurized containers; the prohibition is 'as provided in 2.125', a general FDA rule.

question: If a hairspray uses a chlorofluorocarbon propellant, is the issue only a warning label, or is the propellant itself prohibited?

review.note: The propellant itself is prohibited. 740.11(c) adds that CFC labeling is in 40 CFR 82 (needs_also listed).

question: Does a liquid mouthwash sold off open store shelves need a seal or barrier that shows if someone has opened it?

review.note: (b): liquid oral hygiene products accessible to the public need tamper-resistant packaging.

question: We sell a cosmetic vaginal wash in drugstores with a shrink band printed with our logo around the cap. What must the package say about that band?

review.note: (c): a prominent statement naming the identifying characteristic (logo), unaffected if breached; the shrink-band example is given.

question: Under Part 700, how do we ask FDA to excuse our liquid oral rinse from the tamper-evident package rules, and what must the petition include?

review.note: (d)(1)-(4): citizen petition under 10.30 and its contents.

question: Is a breath-freshening spray in an aerosol can excused from printing a statement that alerts buyers to its tamper-evident feature?

review.note: (c) exempts aerosol products from the labeling statement; (b) defines aerosol product.

question: Can a face cream contain ingredients made from cow brain or spinal cord tissue?

review.note: (a)(5) makes brain and spinal cord SRM for cattle 30 months or older, and (b)(1) bans SRM. The answer depends on age; still answered.

question: We import a Korean serum made with bovine collagen. When filing entry with Customs, what must we affirm, and how quickly must we produce records if asked?

review.note: (c)(6): affirmations at entry; records within 5 days on request.

question: Under Part 700, is rendered beef tallow with 0.12 percent insoluble impurities allowed in a bar soap, and how is that impurity level measured?

review.note: (a)(1)(i) allows tallow at <=0.15% insoluble impurities; (a)(6) gives AOCS Ca 3a-46. Caveat: a true tallow 'soap' sold only as soap is not a cosmetic (701.20), which is a confound for the answer stage.

question: How long must a cosmetic maker keep its cattle-sourcing records, where must they be kept, and are electronic copies acceptable?

review.note: (c)(2)-(4): 2 years, at the establishment or an accessible location, electronic records OK.

question: If our lipstick has UV filters only to keep its color from fading, can the label mention sun protection without the lipstick becoming a drug?

review.note: (a)-(b): sun terminology generally makes the product a drug; a color-protection use is allowed if qualified. 740.19 (suntanning) is unrelated.

question: A hair-color brand adds octinoxate to keep the dye from fading and wants the bottle to say 'with sunscreen.' What extra wording is required, and where?

review.note: (a)-(b): qualifying cosmetic-benefit statement, prominent, with the term.

question: How prominently, and how many times, must the qualifying statement about a cosmetic's sunscreen ingredient appear, and what's an example of acceptable wording?

review.note: (b): prominently, at least once, with the example 'Contains a sunscreen—to protect product color'.

question: Does putting the word 'sunscreen' on a moisturizer's label generally make FDA regulate it as a drug?

review.note: (a): 'generally causes the product to be subject to regulation as a drug'. FD&C 201(g) is only the generic drug definition.

question: Can a shampoo label claim it's gentler than a competitor's baby wash or a medicated cleanser if that comparison isn't true?

review.note: (a): a false representation about another cosmetic or a drug means misbranding. Under FD&C 602(a), false or misleading labeling is misbranding.

question: Our 'Rose & Argan Oil Night Cream' has 14 ingredients, and the rose and argan oils are under 1% each. Is that product name a labeling risk?

review.note: (b): a name featuring some but not all ingredients may mislead; no other section has this rule.

question: Does printing the full ingredient list on the back panel cure a product name that features only some of the ingredients?

review.note: (b) 'even though the names of all such ingredients are stated elsewhere in the labeling'.

question: Marketing wants our serum carton to say it 'works better than prescription retinoid creams.' If that's untrue, is the serum misbranded?

review.note: Under (a), a false comparison with a drug is misbranding; FD&C 602(a) gives the same result generically.

question: Can required label information be printed in tiny type or tucked onto a panel shoppers don't normally see?

review.note: (a)(1) and (a)(6) cover panel placement and small type. FD&C 602(c) is the conspicuousness standard under customary conditions of purchase. 701.10 and 740.2 are narrower (principal display panel, warnings).

question: We sell a body lotion only in Puerto Rico. Can all the mandatory label text be in Spanish instead of English?

review.note: (b)(1): products sold only in Puerto Rico may use the predominant language.

question: Our US carton carries a French tagline, 'Fabriqué avec amour.' Does that mean every required label statement must also appear in French?

review.note: Under (b)(2), any foreign-language representation means all required statements must also appear in that language.

question: If the front of our cosmetic box is crowded with artwork and promotional claims, can that make the required statements legally insufficient?

review.note: (a)(4)-(6): non-required designs and crowding. FD&C 602(c) compares conspicuousness against designs. 701.10 requires the front panel (principal display panel) to carry mandatory info without obscuring designs or crowding.

question: In what order do the components have to be printed on the back of a body lotion, and can our perfume blend simply be called 'fragrance'?

review.note: (a): descending order of predominance; fragrance may be listed as 'fragrance' if within the consumer meaning. 700.3(d) only defines fragrance; 720.4(d)(1) is the voluntary form, not the label; 609(b) fragrance allergens is a future qualifier, not equal.

question: Our three-person brand sells lip balms only through a printed mail-order catalog. Can the full ingredient list appear in the catalog instead of on each tin, and what must go in the shipping box?

review.note: (r): catalog allowed for direct-mail cosmetics; (r)(2) notice in the package (location of lists, mail-on-request statement, distributor name/place) in 3/16-inch letters. No other section covers mail order.

question: A preservative comes along inside the aloe extract we buy and does nothing in our finished cream. Does it have to appear in the ingredient declaration?

review.note: (l)/(l)(1): carry-over incidental ingredient with no function at insignificant level need not be declared. 604(3)(B)(v) 'incidental' is unrelated (hotels/airlines).

question: Under Part 701, can a line of lipstick shades share one label that lists certain colors after 'may contain', even though each tube holds only some of them?

review.note: (g)(2)(i)-(iv): shaded products (lipstick is 720.4(c)(7)), common brand, color additives only; (o)(3) in the same section also covers it. 'Part 701' is a part, not a section number.

question: Does bulk product heading to someone else's plant to be filled and packed need its retail label while it's in transit?

review.note: (a)/(a)(2): exempt in transit and while held if shipped under a written agreement to a plant the shipper does not operate. Writer's alternative 603 only directs FDA to issue such exemptions and omits the agreement condition; weaker, not listed as equal.

question: Our startup ships 500 kg of bulk shampoo base to a contract packer we don't own. What must our written agreement with them contain, and how long do we both keep a copy?

review.note: (a)(2): signed by both, both post-office addresses, specifications ensuring no adulteration/misbranding; each keeps a copy until 2 years after final shipment. 610 (MoCRA records) does not cover this.

question: Our second plant relabels bulk lotion we send it. If a lot is adulterated when it leaves that plant, does the transit relief from label rules still cover the shipment?

review.note: Own plant = (a)(1); (b) voids the exemption ab initio if adulterated or misbranded when removed.

question: What happens to the label relief for a repacking shipment if an FDA investigator asks to see our agreement with the repacker and we refuse?

review.note: (c): refusal by the shipper voids the exemption ab initio as to the shipper; (d)(2) covers refusal by the operator. 704 (inspection) is general, not equal.

question: Which side of a cosmetic carton counts as the 'front' that has to carry the main required label information?

review.note: Undesignated intro defines the principal display panel as the part most likely displayed at retail. 701.2(a)(1) only implies it; not equal.

question: Under Part 701, how do we calculate the front-label area of a round shampoo bottle that is 7 inches tall with a 9-inch circumference?
When measuring the label area of a jar of hair pomade, do we count the lid, the neck and the shoulders of the jar?

review.note: Second '(c)' paragraph (the export gives two paragraphs the path (c)) excludes tops, shoulders and necks of bottles or jars.

question: If a perfume box has two equally prominent faces, either of which might be shown on the shelf, must the required front-label text be repeated on both?

review.note: Intro: info required on the PDP is duplicated on each alternate PDP. 701.2(a)(2) (failure to appear on two or more panels each likely to be displayed) answers equally. 701.13(e) covers net quantity only.

question: Does the front of a cosmetic package have to say what the product actually is, such as 'hand cream' or 'eyeliner'?

review.note: (a) statement of identity on the PDP; (b)(1) common or usual name. 602 has no identity requirement.

question: Our new body shimmer oil is sold as 'Midnight Velvet'. Can that brand-style name stand alone on the front, or must we add a plain descriptive term?

review.note: (b)(2): a fanciful name only when the nature of the cosmetic is obvious; otherwise an appropriately descriptive name.

question: How large, how bold and in what direction must the words telling shoppers what the product is be printed on a lipstick carton's front panel?

review.note: (c): bold type, size reasonably related to the most prominent printed matter, lines parallel to the base.

question: Can a drawing that shows the product being used take the place of words naming the type of cosmetic on the main panel?

review.note: (b)(3): an illustration or vignette representing the intended use may serve.

question: Which firm's identity and address must be shown on a cosmetic's packaging?

review.note: (a): manufacturer, packer or distributor. FD&C 602(b)(1) states the same requirement (writer's alternative, confirmed). 609(a) adverse-event contact is a different requirement.

question: A contract lab in New Jersey makes our vitamin C serum, but only our brand's name appears on the bottle. How should the label describe our connection to the product?

review.note: (c): qualify the name with 'Manufactured for' / 'Distributed by' or similar.

question: We're headquartered in Austin but fill our products at a plant in Ohio. Can the label list only the Austin office as our place of business?

review.note: (e): principal place of business may be stated unless misleading. 'place of business' has only 2 content words and also appears in 602(b) and 701.3(r); not counted as a leak.

question: Does the business address on a cosmetic label need a street and ZIP code, and how is the ZIP handled on packages not meant for consumers?

review.note: (d): street, city, State, ZIP; street omissible if in a current directory; for nonconsumer packages ZIP on label or labeling incl. invoice.

question: Should the amount in a jar of hair gel be stated by weight or by fluid ounces?

review.note: (a): weight for solid, semisolid or viscous products (gel); fluid measure for liquids. 602(b)(2) does not resolve weight vs measure.

question: Our aerosol dry shampoo can holds 5 ounces of product plus propellant. Should the amount printed on the can include the propellant?

review.note: (g)(1): quantity expelled; the propellant is included.

question: What minimum type height applies to the weight statement on a face cream carton whose front panel is 20 square inches?

review.note: (i)(2): PDP over 5 and up to 25 sq in -> at least 1/8 inch.

question: Under Part 701, may we describe our bottle as a 'giant 16 fl oz' size, and can a metric amount also appear on a side panel?

review.note: (f)/(q): no exaggerating qualifiers such as 'giant pint'; (r): a metric statement may appear on the PDP or other panels.

question: When does FDA consider a washing bar to be the traditional fat-and-lye kind that falls outside its cosmetic rules?

review.note: (a)(1)-(2): mostly alkali salts of fatty acids giving the detergency, and labeled/sold only as soap. 201(i) excludes soap but does not define it; not equal.

question: Our handmade lye bar is advertised as 'moisturizing and deodorizing' as well as cleansing. Does that wording change whether FDA regulates it as a cosmetic?

review.note: (a)(2) requires representation only as soap; with cosmetic claims it falls under (b) as a cosmetic. 201(i) is partial.

question: A synthetic cleansing bar that isn't true soap is sold in our gift sets. What statement of the bar's weight does its label need?

review.note: (b): accurate weight of the bar in avoirdupois pounds and ounces, prominently displayed. 701.13 (a),(b),(e),(i) gives the general net-weight rule for a solid cosmetic and answers equally.

question: Under Part 701, is a liquid hand wash built on synthetic surfactants treated as a cosmetic and subject to the cosmetic requirements?

review.note: (b): non-soap body cleansers are cosmetics subject to the act. 'Under Part 701' rules out 201(i), which alone does not settle synthetic surfactants.

question: What should we call the difluoroethane propellant in our hairspray when we print what's in it?

review.note: 1,1-difluoroethane = 'Hydrofluorocarbon 152 A'. 701.3(c)(1) only points to 701.30.

question: Our conditioner uses an ethyl ester made from hydrolyzed collagen, and our chemist wants to list it by its full chemical description. Has FDA set a label name for it?

review.note: Established name 'Ethyl ester of hydrolyzed animal protein' (ester of ethanol and collagen hydrolysate).

question: What label name has FDA assigned to trichlorofluoromethane blended with a trace of nitromethane?

review.note: 'Chlorofluorocarbon 11 S' (text says 0.3 pct nitromethane; 'trace' is loose). 701.3(c)(2)(i)(b) lists 'Chlorofluorocarbon 11S' without the chemical mapping; not equal. 700.23 prohibits CFC propellants, so a full answer should note that; still a plausible lookup.

question: Has FDA itself fixed official ingredient-list names for any aerosol propellants, and if so, which ones?

review.note: Lists CFC 11, 11 S, 12, 114, HCFC 22, 142 B, HFC 152 A. 700.23 (CFC prohibition) is context, not equal.

question: Which companies are asked to sign up their cosmetic plants in FDA's older voluntary program, and does it cost anything?

review.note: Owner/operator of a non-exempt manufacturing or packaging establishment; no fee. 710.9 lists exclusions only (partial). 607 is mandatory MoCRA registration, not the voluntary program.

question: We run a filling plant in Ontario that ships lipsticks to U.S. stores. Does FDA's voluntary establishment program ask us to enroll even though we're outside the country?

review.note: Request extends to foreign establishments whose products are exported for sale in any State.

question: Our cream is made and sold only within Oregon. Does FDA's voluntary request to enroll production sites still reach a plant whose goods never cross state lines?

review.note: 'whether or not the product enters interstate commerce'.

question: Under Part 710, does a company that runs three cosmetic plants register once or separately for each plant?

review.note: 710.1 'register for each such establishment'; 710.4 'given separately for each establishment' answers equally (writer's alternative, confirmed). 607(a)(1) is MoCRA; Part 710 is named.

question: How soon after a new cosmetics plant starts running should it be signed up in FDA's voluntary establishment program?

review.note: Within 30 days after operation begins. 607(a)(1)(B) (60 days, mandatory) answers a different question; this one says voluntary.

question: Our contract packing line in Georgia began filling body washes on March 3. Under the voluntary FD-2511 program, by what date should the site be enrolled?

review.note: 30 days from March 3 = April 2. A form number is not a section number.

question: For the voluntary establishment program, is the sign-up window counted from when we lease the building or from when production actually begins?

review.note: Counted from when the operation begins.

question: What is the recommended deadline for an owner to submit Form FD-2511 for a newly opened cosmetic establishment?

review.note: 30 days. 710.2 does not name FD-2511, but the form ties the question to Part 710 (710.3-710.7 name it).

question: Where can we pick up the paper form for FDA's voluntary cosmetic plant enrollment, and where do we mail it back?

review.note: Form from FDA College Park or any district office; mail to Cosmetic Product Establishment Registration, College Park. 'and where' is 2 function words.

question: Our office manager has never handled FDA paperwork. Can she get the establishment enrollment form for our lotion workshop from a nearby FDA district office?

review.note: 'or at any Food and Drug Administration district office'.

question: What mailing address goes on the envelope for a completed voluntary cosmetic establishment registration form?

review.note: Mailing address stated in full.

question: What is the procedure for submitting a voluntary cosmetic establishment registration, and which form is used?

review.note: Form FD-2511, obtained from FDA or a district office, mailed to College Park. 710.4 names the form only (partial).

question: What details does FDA's voluntary cosmetic plant sign-up form ask for?

review.note: Name and address with ZIP, all business trading names, type of business. 607(b)(2) is the mandatory registration; question says voluntary.

question: We sell under three brand names, 'Lumi', 'Kora' and 'Bay & Birch', all made at one site. Should each name go on our voluntary establishment registration form?

review.note: 'all business trading names used by the establishment'; 700.3(m) (needs_also) defines trading names as label names owned by the manufacturer/packer.

question: If we fill product at two addresses in the same city, do we report the details once or separately for each site on the voluntary form?

review.note: Separately for each establishment as defined in 700.3(j) (needs_also). 710.1 'register for each such establishment' is equal (writer's alternative, confirmed).

question: On Form FD-2511, how do we show whether our business manufactures the products or only packs them?

review.note: The form asks for 'type of business (manufacturer and/or packer)'.

question: We moved our cosmetics plant to a new address. How quickly should our voluntary FDA establishment record be updated?

review.note: A new FD-2511 within 30 days of the change. 607(a)(4) (60 days) is the mandatory regime; question says voluntary.

question: Sunrise Botanicals LLC renamed itself Solace Skin LLC on June 1 and stopped using the old name. What should it file with FDA's voluntary program, and by when?

review.note: A new FD-2511 within 30 days; the text says it is also needed to cancel when the old name is no longer used.

question: Does FDA's voluntary establishment program expect a brand-new form, or just a letter, when details we filed have changed?

review.note: A new Form FD-2511, not a letter.

question: What is the time limit for amending a submitted Form FD-2511 after our trade names change?

review.note: 30 days. 720.6 (60 days) concerns Form 2512 brand names, not FD-2511.

question: Once FDA processes our voluntary cosmetic plant sign-up, what do we receive back from the agency?

review.note: A validated copy of FD-2511 and a permanent registration number.

question: Our head office is in Miami but we enrolled only our Tampa filling plant. Where will FDA send the validated proof of enrollment?

review.note: Sent only to the location shown for the registering establishment (Tampa).

question: Is the number given to a voluntarily enrolled cosmetic establishment temporary, or does it stay with the site permanently?

review.note: 'A permanent registration number will be assigned'. No 3-word heading overlap.

question: How does FDA notify a firm that its cosmetic establishment registration has been accepted?

review.note: Validated copy of FD-2511. The question omits 'voluntary', so a reader may mean MoCRA registration, but 607 says nothing about notification beyond assigning a number; 710.6 is the only answer in the corpus. Adding 'voluntary' would remove the ambiguity.

question: Can anyone look at the voluntary plant form a competitor sent to FDA, and where would we go to see it?

review.note: Filed FD-2511 is available for inspection at FDA, 5001 Campus Dr., College Park.

question: Our law firm is doing due diligence on a lotion maker we may acquire. Can we review the establishment form it filed under FDA's voluntary program?

review.note: Yes, a copy is available for inspection at FDA College Park.

question: At which FDA location are copies of filed cosmetic establishment registration forms kept for review?

review.note: FDA, 5001 Campus Dr., College Park, MD.

question: Are voluntary cosmetic establishment registrations kept confidential, or are they open to inspection at FDA?

review.note: Open to inspection. 607(e) confidentiality applies to mandatory registrations only; the question says voluntary.

question: Can we tell customers our skincare factory is 'FDA approved' because we enrolled it with the agency?

review.note: Registration does not denote approval; a representation implying approval is misleading. 602(a) is general; 720.9 is for ingredient statements.

question: Our online listing for a beard oil shows a badge reading 'Made in an FDA-registered plant, No. 12345'. We did voluntarily enroll the plant. Is that badge a problem?

review.note: Badge citing registration and number is misleading if it creates an impression of official approval.

question: Does being given an establishment number by FDA mean the agency has checked and okayed our products?

review.note: No 'voluntary', but 607 says nothing about approval; 710.8 is the only answer.

question: Would featuring our cosmetic plant's FDA registration number in a TV advertisement be considered misleading?

review.note: Misleading if it creates an impression of approval (labeling or advertising). 'registration number' is only 2 heading words. Same MoCRA ambiguity as 710.8-3, no competing section.

question: Does a hair salon that mixes its own color treatments in-house need to sign up with FDA's voluntary cosmetic plant program?

review.note: (a) beauty shops compounding at a single location and administering there. 604(3)(B)(i) is the MoCRA facility exclusion, not the voluntary program.

question: A university lab makes small batches of experimental lotion for teaching and never sells them. Is it expected to enroll in FDA's voluntary establishment program?

review.note: (c) research/teaching, not sold. 604(3)(B)(vii) is MoCRA, not the voluntary program.

question: Are dermatology clinics that prepare creams for their own patients left out of the voluntary establishment registration program?

review.note: (b) physicians, hospitals, clinics. 604(3)(B)(iii) is MoCRA.

question: Under Part 710, which kinds of businesses are not asked to register their cosmetic establishments?

review.note: Lists (a)-(c).

question: Who is supposed to send FDA the voluntary formula disclosure for a cosmetic: the maker, the packer or the brand owner?

review.note: Either the manufacturer, packer or distributor (brand owner = distributor).

question: We're a Korean brand exporting sheet masks for sale in California. Does FDA's voluntary ingredient statement program extend to foreign distributors like us?

review.note: Extends to foreign manufacturers, packers or distributors exporting for sale in any State.

question: Is there any charge for submitting a voluntary cosmetic ingredient statement, and does it matter that our lip gloss is sold in one state only?

review.note: No filing fee; whether or not the product enters interstate commerce.

question: Under Part 720, may the distributor named on the label file the ingredient statement instead of the manufacturer?

review.note: Either may file. 720.4(a)(1)-(2) is consistent but partial.

question: How long after a new cosmetic hits store shelves should the voluntary formula paperwork reach FDA?

review.note: 60 days after commercial distribution begins. Per 700.3(i), 'commercial distribution' means over $1,000 in annual sales, not shelf placement. 607(c)(2) (120-day listing) is mandatory MoCRA.

question: We've sold only $600 worth of a trial lip scrub so far this year. Has the clock for filing its voluntary ingredient statement started running?

review.note: The clock is in 720.2 (60 days after commercial distribution begins), but the $600 answer depends on 700.3(i) (over $1,000 annual gross sales), which is listed in needs_also.

question: We already had 40 products on the market when FDA's voluntary ingredient program took effect. How long were we given to submit statements for them?

review.note: Within 180 days after forms were made available to industry (not from the effective date).

question: When should Form FDA 2512 be submitted for a cosmetic first sold after the program's effective date?

review.note: Within 60 days after commercial distribution begins.

question: Which FDA office receives completed voluntary formula statements for cosmetics, and how can we get blank copies?

review.note: Mailed or delivered to Cosmetic Product Statement, FDA, College Park; blank forms from FDA or any district office.

question: We're pulling a discontinued eyeliner shade off the market and want to tell FDA's voluntary program. Which form do we use, and can it be hand-delivered?

review.note: Form FDA 2514; 'mailed or delivered'. Writer's alternative 720.6 names Form 2514 and the 180-day deadline but not delivery; partial, not listed as equal.

question: Can a completed cosmetic ingredient statement be dropped off in person at FDA rather than mailed?

review.note: 'mailed or delivered'.

question: Under Part 720, how and where are the ingredient statement forms submitted to FDA?

review.note: 'how and where' echoes the heading 'How and where to file' but is only function words; not counted as a leak. Generic but answerable.

question: What does FDA's voluntary formula statement ask a cosmetic company to disclose about each product?
We make a liquid foundation in 18 shades that differ only in pigment amounts. Do we need a separate voluntary ingredient statement for every shade?

review.note: (e): one form may cover shades that differ only in color-additive amounts (hair colorants excepted). 607(c)(4)(B) is the MoCRA listing; the question says voluntary.

question: A dermatologist treating a patient's rash asks us for the ingredients and a sample of our night cream. What does the voluntary filing program expect us to provide?

review.note: (b)(4): ingredient info and, when requested, samples to a licensed physician treating a patient.

question: Which product category should an indoor tanning lotion be listed under on the voluntary cosmetic ingredient statement?

review.note: (c)(13)(ii) Indoor tanning preparations. 740.19 defines suntanning preparations for the warning, not filing categories.

question: We swapped one preservative in our conditioner. How soon should our voluntary formula record at FDA be updated?

review.note: Ingredient change: amended 2512 within 60 days after the product enters commercial distribution.

question: Our company stopped selling a peppermint foot lotion, and the person who files our FDA paperwork learned of it on July 10. When is the notice due, and on which form?

review.note: Form FDA 2514 within 180 days after the filer learns of the discontinuance (July 10). 720.3 names Form 2514 but gives no deadline; partial.

question: Apart from ingredient or brand-name changes, how quickly should other corrections to a filed cosmetic ingredient statement be sent in?

review.note: Within a year.

question: What is the deadline to amend Form FDA 2512 after we rename a product's brand?

review.note: Brand-name change: amended 2512 within 60 days after entry into commercial distribution.

question: Do we get some kind of ID number back after sending FDA our cosmetic's formula voluntarily?

review.note: A permanent statement number or an FDA reference number.

question: We mailed an ingredient statement for our clay mask but forgot to have it signed. Will FDA just reject it, or tell us what's missing?

review.note: FDA notifies how the statement is incomplete; the signature requirement is 720.4(b)(2), listed in needs_also.

question: In what situation does FDA give a cosmetic ingredient statement a reference number rather than a permanent statement number?

review.note: The rule says only 'in those cases where a permanent number cannot be assigned'; no further criteria anywhere in the corpus. Thin but correct.

question: Who receives FDA's acknowledgment notice when a cosmetic product ingredient statement is filed?

review.note: Notice goes to the individual who signed the statement. Repeats 'cosmetic product ingredient statement' (4 heading words), but 'cosmetic product' is generic and the phrase is the Form 2512 name used across Part 720; only 2 distinctive words. Borderline: 'voluntary ingredient statement' would be safer.

question: How do we ask FDA to keep one proprietary component of our perfume oil from being made public, and what must the request include?

review.note: (a)-(c): request with factual and legal grounds addressing the (b) factors, plus a statement that the identity was not previously disclosed. 701.3(a) 'and other ingredients' applies only after acceptance.

question: FDA tentatively denied our request to keep a novel peptide's identity secret, and the letter arrived March 4. How long do we have to send more data and ask for reconsideration?

review.note: (e): 60 days from receipt of the tentative denial (by May 3).

question: If FDA finally decides our ingredient isn't a trade secret, what can we do to stop its disclosure, and how fast must we act?

review.note: (g): sue within 30 calendar days; FDA withholds disclosure until the courts decide.

question: What factors does FDA weigh when deciding whether a cosmetic ingredient's identity qualifies as a trade secret?

review.note: (b)(1)-(6). 71.15 concerns color-additive petitions; not equal.

question: Can our toner's box say 'formula disclosed to FDA' because we voluntarily sent the agency our ingredient list?

review.note: A representation implying official approval because of the filing is misleading.

question: A distributor wants our sell sheet to show the FDA-assigned statement number for our lash conditioner to reassure buyers. Could that be read as implying FDA approval?

review.note: Using the statement number to imply approval is misleading. 'statement number' is only 2 heading words.

question: Does FDA's assigning a number to our cosmetic formula submission mean the agency has approved the product?

review.note: Filing or the number does not denote approval. 710.8 is the establishment-number counterpart, not this.

question: Is it misleading to advertise that a cosmetic's ingredient statement has been filed with FDA?

review.note: Misleading if it creates an impression of official approval.

question: Who decides when a cosmetic label needs a caution about health risks: the company, or only FDA through a rule?

review.note: (a) duty to warn whenever necessary, without a specific rule; (b) FDA may also prescribe warnings by rule.

question: Our new hot-wax hair remover could burn skin if overheated, but no regulation names a caution for it. Must we put one on the label anyway?

review.note: (a): a warning is required whenever necessary to prevent a health hazard.

question: What must a petition asking FDA to require a new cosmetic caution contain before it is published for comment?

review.note: (b): adequate factual basis, part 10 form; published if it contains reasonable grounds.

question: Under Part 740, can FDA propose a mandatory warning for a cosmetic on its own initiative, without anyone petitioning?

review.note: (b) 'on his own initiative'.

question: Can the safety caution on our spray tan bottle be printed in light gray text on a pale background?

review.note: (a): bold type on a contrasting background. 701.2(a)(6) (insufficient background contrast) is a general, weaker answer; not listed as equal.

question: Our nail art pens are only 3 inches long and the required caution won't fit at the normal minimum size. Is there any route to using smaller type?

review.note: (b): FDA may allow smaller type by regulation on petition.

question: Where does a request to allow smaller-than-standard type for a cosmetic's warning get sent, and in what format?

review.note: (b): petition to the Dockets Management Staff in the part 10 form.

question: What is the minimum letter height for a warning statement on a cosmetic label?

review.note: (a): 1/16 inch. 'warning statement' is only 2 heading words. 701.3(b) 1/16 inch is for ingredient lists, not warnings.

question: If we can't yet back up that our new serum is harmless, what must its front label say before we sell it?

review.note: (a): 'Warning-The safety of this product has not been determined.' on the PDP. 601(g) (needs_also) now makes an unsubstantiated product adulterated anyway.

question: A botanical extract we've used in toners for 15 years is now questioned by one inconclusive study, and we've commissioned new tests. Must we add the 'safety not determined' warning meanwhile?

review.note: (b)(1)-(3): history-of-use relief if previously substantiated, no demonstrated hazard, and studies under way.

question: If our ingredient qualifies for the history-of-use relief from the unproven-safety warning, are we also protected from adulteration charges?

review.note: (c): not an exemption from the adulteration provisions.

question: Does FDA expect every ingredient and the finished cosmetic to have its safety supported before it goes on the market?

review.note: (a): each ingredient and the finished product substantiated before marketing. 608(a),(c) and 601(g) state the same duty for the product and each ingredient (without 'prior to marketing'); equal. 608 was the writer's alternative.

question: Under Part 740, what caution has to be printed on an aerosol can of hairspray?

review.note: (a)(1) standard warning; (b)(1) inhalation warning if the propellant is a halocarbon or hydrocarbon.

question: Our children's spray-on glitter comes in a pressurized can with butane propellant. Can we add 'except under adult supervision' to the warning, and is the inhaling caution needed too?

review.note: (a)(2) 'except under adult supervision' allowed; (b)(1) needed because butane is a hydrocarbon.

question: Our shaving foam contains 6 percent hydrocarbon propellant. Does it need the warning about deliberately inhaling the contents?

review.note: (b)(2)(i): foam with less than 10% propellant is exempt.

question: For a pressurized mousse packed in a glass bottle and not dispensed as a spray, which words of the standard warning may be changed or left out?

review.note: (a)(3) 'break' for 'puncture' in glass; (a)(4) drop 'Avoid spraying in eyes'.

question: What caution does FDA require on a deodorizing mist for women's intimate areas?

review.note: (b) caution text.

question: Marketing wants to call our all-over deodorant body mist 'the hygienic choice for women'. Is that wording allowed?

review.note: (a) all-over-body spray is covered; (c) 'hygienic' misbrands.

question: Our pump-spray feminine deodorant contains no liquefied gas propellant. Can we drop the line about spraying at least 8 inches from skin?

review.note: (b): the 8-inch sentence is not needed without a liquefied gas propellant. 'feminine deodorant' is only 2 heading words.

question: Which products count as a feminine deodorant spray for purposes of FDA's caution requirement?

review.note: Leak: 'feminine deodorant spray' copies the whole 3-word heading 'Feminine deodorant sprays'. Gold otherwise right ((a) genital-area or all-over-body spray deodorants). Salvage with e.g. 'intimate-area deodorizing mist'.

question: What caution has to be printed on a bubble bath?

review.note: (b) caution and directions; not for products labeled for adults only.

question: We sell a luxury bath foam marketed strictly to adults as a spa product. Do we still need the caution about skin and urinary tract irritation?

review.note: (b): exempt only if labeled as intended exclusively for adults ('marketed' alone is not enough).

question: For a kids' bubble bath, can the line about keeping it away from children be extended to mention adult supervision?
Does a fizzing bath bomb that includes a surfactant to make foam count as a product needing the bath-foam caution?

review.note: (a): added to a bath to produce foam, contains a surface-active agent.

question: Which hair color ingredients trigger a label caution saying they caused tumors in lab animals?

review.note: (b): 2,4-diaminoanisole and its sulfate. The 601(a) caution is about irritation and blindness, not cancer.

question: Our salon-brand permanent dye contains 2,4-diaminoanisole sulfate. What exact warning must appear, and on which parts of the packaging?

review.note: (a): warning text, on the PDP and any accompanying labeling; 740.2 is in needs_also. The 601(a)/70.3(u) patch-test caution also applies to coal-tar dyes, so a full answer may mention it.

question: Is 4-methoxy-m-phenylenediamine one of the dye intermediates covered by the skin-penetration cancer warning rule?
Besides the carton's front panel, must the cancer warning for a coal tar hair dye with 2,4-diaminoanisole also appear in the instruction leaflet?

review.note: Leak: 'coal tar hair dye' copies 4 consecutive heading words ('Coal tar hair dyes ...'). Gold fine ((a): PDP and any accompanying labeling). Salvage with e.g. 'permanent hair dye containing 2,4-diaminoanisole'.

question: What warning goes on a bronzing oil with no SPF that people use while lying in the sun?

review.note: Warning text; a bronzing oil used while UV tanning is a suntanning preparation.

question: We sell a dihydroxyacetone self-tanning mousse with no sunscreen. Does it need the 'does not protect against sunburn' warning even though customers never sunbathe with it?

review.note: The definition expressly includes DHA color-imparting products used without UV exposure. 73.2150 (DHA listing) has no such warning.

question: Does the sunscreen-free tanning warning rule apply to a lotion that is itself sold to protect against sunburn?

review.note: Excludes products intended to provide sun protection. 700.35 (sunscreen terms make it a drug) is partial.

question: Under Part 740, which products count as suntanning preparations for the no-sunscreen warning?

review.note: Definition is in the text. 'suntanning preparations' reproduces the whole 2-word heading: not a leak under the 3-word rule, but an easy lexical match.

question: Does the federal meaning of 'cosmetic' cover ingredients we sell to other brands for their creams, or only finished products people put on their bodies?

review.note: 201(i)(2) 'articles intended for use as a component of any such articles' answers it. 700.3(h) defines 'cosmetic raw material' and 700.3(b) defines 'cosmetic product' as finished, but neither says whether an ingredient is a 'cosmetic', so they are not equal. 604(2) is the MoCRA 'cosmetic product' definition and is not equal either.

question: Our new serum's box says it 'reduces inflammation and repairs damaged skin cells.' Could those claims make FDA treat it as a drug rather than a beauty product?

review.note: 201(g)(1)(B) disease treatment/mitigation and (C) structure/function versus (i) cosmetic. grep 'structure or any function|cure, mitigation' finds only 201 plus 740.19, a suntanning warning that is not equal.

question: When FDA judges whether our shampoo's labeling is misleading, can it count important risks we failed to mention, not just what the label actually says?

review.note: 201(n): misleading is judged by the extent to which the labeling fails to reveal material facts and consequences of use. 602(a) only says false/misleading labeling misbrands, without the omission rule. 701.1 does not cover omissions.

question: Under the FD&C Act, what is the difference between a 'label' and 'labeling', and does a leaflet packed inside the carton count as labeling?

review.note: 201(k) label = immediate container; (m) labeling includes matter 'accompanying such article', so an insert counts. grep finds no other definition of labeling.

question: Can we still make and ship a face wash that uses tiny plastic beads to scrub the skin, if customers rinse it off?

review.note: 301(ddd)(1) bans the manufacture and interstate introduction of rinse-off cosmetics with plastic microbeads; (2)(A) defines a microbead as under 5 mm and used to exfoliate/cleanse. grep 'microbead' finds only 301.

question: A store in Ohio peeled our ingredient stickers off lipsticks it bought from us and relabeled them before putting them on the shelf. Is the store breaking federal law?

review.note: 301(k): removing labeling while the item is held for sale after interstate shipment is prohibited if it results in misbranding. That missing ingredient labels misbrand the product comes from 602/701.3, which is implied but not needed. grep 'obliterat|removal of the whole' finds only 301.

question: If FDA orders our company to stop distributing a contaminated shampoo and we keep shipping it anyway, is defying that order itself a violation?

review.note: 301(iii) prohibits failing to follow an order 'under section 364g'. You need 611(a)/(d) (needs_also 611, confirmed) to know a cease-distribution order is a 364g order. 611 alone does not say that defying the order is a prohibited act, so it is not equal.

question: Which acts involving an adulterated or mislabeled cosmetic are banned: shipping it across state lines, receiving it, or causing the problem while it is in commerce?

review.note: 301(a) introduction into interstate commerce, (b) adulterating/misbranding while in commerce, (c) receipt. All three are prohibited. No other section restates them.

question: Is a cream legally considered tainted if it was mixed in a dirty plant, even if no one has been harmed yet?

review.note: 601(c) applies to insanitary conditions 'whereby it may have become contaminated', so no harm is needed. 704(b)(1) uses the same words only for an inspector's report and is not equal.

question: Our permanent hair color uses a coal-tar dye that can irritate some people's skin. If the box carries the patch-test caution and directions, are we protected from the harmful-ingredient rule?

review.note: 601(a) coal-tar hair dye exception: the caution legend plus adequate patch-test directions. 740.18 (cancer warning) and 608(b) (safety-substantiation exemption) are different rules and not equal.

question: Our jar supplier switched to a plastic that leaches a harmful chemical into the cream. Can the container alone make the product unlawful?

review.note: 601(d): a container made of a poisonous/deleterious substance that may make the contents injurious. grep 'container is composed|deleterious' finds only ingredient bans in 700.x, which are not equal.

question: Does a cosmetic become adulterated if it lacks adequate safety support for its ingredients or was made outside the required manufacturing practices?

review.note: 601(f) GMP and 601(g) substantiation answer it alone. The writer's needs_also 608/606 are only background definitions and are not needed for the yes/no answer.

question: Must a packaged cosmetic show who made or sold it and how much product is inside, or is that optional?

review.note: 602(b)(1)-(2) covers both name/place and quantity. 701.12(a) (name and place of business) and 701.13(a) (net quantity) each cover one half. As a pair they answer it equally, so accept either one or both.

question: We put a 30 ml serum bottle in a carton sized for 100 ml so it stands out on the shelf. Can the oversized box itself get the product in trouble?

review.note: 602(d): a container 'so made, formed, or filled as to be misleading'. grep 'slack|nonfunctional|so made, formed' finds only 602; the corpus has no slack-fill regulation.

question: Our nail glue remover is subject to the child-resistant packaging rules for poisons. If we ship it with an ordinary cap, does that also make it unlawful as a cosmetic?

review.note: 602(f): packaging/labeling that violates a regulation under 15 U.S.C. 1472/1473 (poison prevention packaging) misbrands. grep 'child.resistant|1472|1473' finds only 602.

question: Is a color additive package mislabeled if it doesn't follow the color additive packaging and labeling regulations, and are colors sold only for hair dyes excepted?

review.note: 602(e) answers both parts, including the hair-dye exception. 70.20/70.25 state the packaging/labeling requirements but do not say that non-conformity misbrands, and they mention the hair-dye exclusion only in their headings, so they are not equal. needs_also 70.25 is not needed.

question: Is there a legal basis for leaving consumer labels off cosmetics that will be filled and labeled at another company's plant?

review.note: 603 is the statutory basis: FDA 'shall promulgate regulations exempting' cosmetics processed/labeled/repacked at another establishment. 701.9(a)(2) is the operative exemption and adds the written-agreement condition for another company's plant. Both are acceptable.

question: Our Texas plant ships shampoo in 1,000-liter totes to a Georgia co-packer that bottles and labels it. Do the totes need full retail labeling while in transit?

review.note: 603 only tells FDA to write an exemption. 701.9(a) actually exempts shipments 'during the time of introduction into and movement in interstate commerce' from the 601(a)/602(b) labeling requirements. For a different-company co-packer it requires a signed written agreement ((a)(2)), and the exemption is void if the goods are adulterated/misbranded on removal ((d)(1)). 603 can remain an acceptable secondary answer.

question: What condition attaches to the bulk-shipment label exemption, and what must be true of the cosmetic once it leaves the repacking site?

review.note: 603: the condition is that the cosmetic is not adulterated/misbranded on removal from the repacking establishment. 701.9 gives the fuller set of conditions (operator, or written agreement in (a)(1)/(a)(2)) and the void-ab-initio rule on removal ((b), (d)(1)). Accept either.

question: Is FDA required by the FD&C Act to issue rules exempting cosmetics repacked in quantity at a second site from labeling requirements?

review.note: Only 603 states the statutory mandate ('The Secretary shall promulgate regulations exempting...'). 701.9 implements it but does not state the mandate, so it is not equal. Heading 'Regulations making exemptions' is not copied ('issue rules exempting').

question: Who is legally on the hook as the company answerable for a cosmetic: the factory that makes it or the brand named on the label?

review.note: 604(4): the responsible person is the manufacturer, packer or distributor whose name appears on the label. 701.12(c) covers only the 'Manufactured for/Distributed by' wording and does not assign responsibility.

question: We run a hair salon that blends its own conditioner in a back room and also sells retail brands made elsewhere. Does that make the salon a cosmetics facility under the 2022 cosmetics law?

review.note: 604(3)(A) facility; (3)(B)(i) salons are excluded unless they manufacture/process at that location, which this one does. 710.9(a) is the pre-MoCRA voluntary-registration exemption for beauty shops and is not equal for the 2022 law.

question: Our warehouse only relabels and repacks cosmetics, but it also fills empty bottles from bulk drums. Does the filling take it out of the relabel-and-repack carve-out?

review.note: 604(3)(B)(viii) excludes establishments that solely label/relabel/package/repackage; (3)(C) says packaging/repackaging does not include filling containers, so filling takes the warehouse out of the exclusion. grep 'filling a product container|relabel' finds only 604.

question: What outcomes make a reaction to a cosmetic 'serious' in the legal sense? Do an infection, significant hair loss, or needing surgery to prevent harm count?

review.note: 604(5)(A)(vi) infection, (A)(vii) significant hair loss, (B) medical or surgical intervention. 700.3(q) 'reportable experience' is the old voluntary concept and is not equal.

question: If a customer is hospitalized after using our face cream, what do we have to send FDA, and by when?

review.note: 605(a)/(b)(1): the serious adverse event report plus a copy of the label within 15 business days. That hospitalization makes the event serious comes from 604(5)(A)(iii), which is supporting only.

question: We are a small skincare brand under $1 million in yearly U.S. sales, making only wash-off cleansers. A customer wrote in about a rash. How many years must we keep that file?

review.note: 605(e)(1) gives 6 years, or 3 for a small business that does not make 364h(b) products. The $1M threshold and the product categories (rinse-off cleansers are not among them) are in 612, so needs_also 612 is confirmed and required.

question: FDA suspects something in our perfume blend caused a serious reaction and asked in writing for the fragrance ingredients. How soon must we respond, and will the list stay out of FOIA releases?

review.note: 605(f): a written request, a response within 30 days, and the list is withheld under FOIA 552(b)(3). grep 'fragrance or flavor|allergen' finds 609(b) and 701.3(a), but neither covers this.

question: Does filing a serious reaction report with FDA amount to admitting our product caused the injury, and may we attach a statement denying that?

review.note: 605(h)(4): submission is not an admission; (g)(1) allows an accompanying denial statement. grep 'admission' finds only 605.

question: Does FDA have to write factory quality standards for cosmetic makers, and should they line up with international standards like ISO 22716?

review.note: 606(a): FDA 'shall by regulation establish' GMP consistent with national and international standards. ISO 22716 is not named, which is fine. grep 'international standards' finds only 606.

question: We're a five-person lotion workshop. Will the coming cosmetics manufacturing quality rules be simpler for a firm our size, or give us longer to comply?

review.note: 606(b): simplified GMP for smaller businesses and possibly longer compliance times. needs_also 612 is relevant: firms with sales under $1M that do not make 612(b) products are exempt from 364b entirely. The question gives headcount, not sales.

question: By what dates was FDA supposed to propose and then finalize the cosmetics manufacturing quality rule after the December 2022 law?

review.note: 606(c): proposed rule within 2 years and final rule within 3 years after Dec 29, 2022. grep 'proposed rulemaking' also finds 609(b), the fragrance-allergen rule, which is not equal.

question: During an inspection, may FDA review our batch records to check whether we follow its manufacturing standards for cosmetics?

review.note: 606(a): GMP regulations may allow records inspection during a 374 inspection. 704(a)(1) confirmed: for a cosmetic facility, the inspection 'shall extend to all records... described in sections 364a, 364b, and 364f' when the standard applies. The writer's alternate holds.

question: Is our cosmetics plant required to sign up with FDA, and how often does that sign-up have to be renewed?

review.note: 607(a)(1)(A)/(B) require registration; (a)(2) requires biennial renewal. 710.x is the voluntary scheme and is not equal. Caveat: 612(a) exempts small businesses from 364c and 613 exempts drug-cosmetics, so 'required' depends on the firm.

question: We first sold a new tinted moisturizer across state lines on April 15, 2025. By what date must the mandatory product listing reach FDA?

review.note: 607(c)(2): within 120 days of first marketing in interstate commerce, i.e. Aug 13, 2025. grep '120 days' finds only 607. 720.2 covers voluntary CPIS timing and is not equal.

question: FDA told us it intends to suspend our plant's registration over a mold problem. How many days do we have to send a fix plan, and how soon is the hearing?

review.note: 607(f)(2)(B): a plan within 5 business days of the notice; (f)(3): a hearing no later than 5 business days after the order. grep 'suspen' finds only color-certification suspension (80.34, 82.3) and 704 accreditation, which are not equal.

question: What must each cosmetic product listing contain under the FD&C Act, and can one listing cover shades that differ only in color or fragrance?

review.note: 607(c)(4)(A) lists the contents; (c)(4)(B) allows one flexible listing for products that differ only in color, fragrance, flavor or quantity. 720.4 covers voluntary CPIS contents and is not equal. 'product listing' is only 2 heading words, so there is no leak.

question: What proof do we need that our lip scrub is safe before it goes on sale, and must we keep that evidence on file?

review.note: 608(a) requires substantiation and records; (c)(1) defines the evidence. The writer's alternate 740.10 is only partial: it covers the pre-marketing substantiation duty and the warning, but not what proof is needed or records. Not equal; treat it as a weak secondary answer at most.

question: Some users of our new exfoliating peel pad feel brief tingling and mild redness that fades within an hour. Does that alone make the product unsafe in FDA's eyes?

review.note: 608(c)(2): FDA shall not consider a product injurious solely because of minor and transient reactions or skin irritation. No other section has this rule.

question: For a coal-tar hair dye that already carries the patch-test caution, are we excused from the new safety-proof duty, and what files must we still keep?

review.note: 608(b): (a) does not apply to a coal-tar hair dye that complies with 361(a), but safety records must still be kept. 601(a) (needs_also) supplies the caution-legend condition.

question: What counts as 'adequate substantiation of safety'? Must it be our own clinical testing, or can expert review of published ingredient data be enough?

review.note: 608(c)(1): tests, studies, research, analyses or other evidence that qualified experts consider sufficient, so in-house clinical testing is not required. The quoted term comes from the definition, not the heading ('Safety substantiation'), so there is no leak. 740.10 uses the term without defining it.

question: Does our cosmetic packaging have to give customers a way to reach us about bad reactions, and can a website address count?

review.note: 609(a): the label must include a domestic address, phone or electronic contact, 'which may include a website'. 605(d) only says reports are received through that contact and is not equal. 701.12 covers the place of business, not AE contact.

question: We sell a gel-polish system only to licensed nail technicians through beauty distributors. What statement must the product's label carry about who may use it?

review.note: 609(c)(2)(A): a clear and prominent statement that the product is to be used only by licensed professionals. grep 'licensed|professional' finds nothing else relevant to cosmetics.

question: Would a freelance makeup artist without a state license count as a 'professional' for products marked for professional use only?

review.note: 609(c)(1): a professional must be licensed by a State in cosmetology, nail care, barbering or esthetics, so an unlicensed freelancer does not count.

question: Must each fragrance allergen in our body mist be named on the label, and how will FDA decide which substances and threshold amounts apply?

review.note: 609(b): each fragrance allergen must be identified; substances are set by regulation, considering EU/State rules, with possible thresholds. 701.3(a), which allows 'fragrance' as a collective name, is the contrasting current rule and is not equal.

question: When can FDA demand to see and copy our company files about a cosmetic it thinks could seriously hurt people?

review.note: 610(a): a reasonable belief that the product is likely adulterated and presents a threat of serious adverse health consequences/death triggers access and copying. 704(a)(1) extends cosmetic inspections to 364f records but does not state the trigger, so it is not equal.

question: We are a contract filler for a brand whose eye cream FDA suspects is contaminated with bacteria that could cause serious injury. Can FDA require us, not only the brand, to let it copy batch documents?

review.note: 610(a): 'each responsible person and facility shall... permit' access, so the contract filler, as a facility, is covered.

question: Does the special document-access power for dangerous cosmetics cut back FDA's other authority to inspect our adverse-event and manufacturing files?

review.note: 610(b) rule of construction: it does not limit other records authority, including 364a (adverse events) and 364b (GMP).

question: Which kinds of company data are off-limits under the FD&C Act when FDA requests cosmetic records: formulas, pricing, safety substantiation data, or shipment data?

review.note: 610(a), last sentence: formulas and pricing are excluded; safety substantiation data and shipment data are carved back in. The 704(a)(1) exclusion list applies to drug/device/tobacco inspections and omits formulas and substantiation, so it is not equal.

question: If FDA believes one of our body lotions could seriously injure or kill someone, can it force us to stop shipping it, or is pulling it always our own call?

review.note: 611(a): voluntary cease first, then FDA may order cessation. Grep 'cease distribution|recall': 607(f) (facility registration suspension) is related but needs belief other products are affected, so it is not an equal answer; 301(iii) only makes ignoring the order a prohibited act.

question: FDA contacted our 12-person eye cream company about a contaminated lot that could cause serious harm and asked us to halt distribution voluntarily. We missed the deadline they set. What can the agency do now, and what happens after its order?

review.note: 611(a) order after the missed deadline; 611(b) hearing within 10 days, (c) vacate/continue/amend to recall, (d) duty to comply. gold_paragraphs should add (b) and (d). '12-person' is a good distractor: 612 exempts small businesses only from 364b/364c, not from 611. 301(iii) is complementary (failing to follow the order is a prohibited act).

question: After an FDA order forces a cosmetic off store shelves, what must the agency's public announcement include: the product name, the risk, a photo, information on similar items that aren't affected?

review.note: 611(f)(1)(B)(i)-(iii) and (f)(2). The question lists the statutory items almost verbatim ('similar items that aren't affected' ~ (f)(1)(B)(iii)), so it is leading but has no heading or number leak. The photo is 'as appropriate ... if available', not a strict must. (f) applies to a recall under this section; 'forces off shelves' is close enough. No other section has press-release/public-notice content (grep).

question: We received an FDA order to stop distributing our hair serum. Within how many days must our informal hearing be held?

review.note: 611(b): not later than 10 days after the order. Confusable distractor: 607(f)(3) gives a 5-business-day hearing, but for a facility registration suspension, not for a product cease-distribution order. 201(x) defines 'informal hearing' with no day count. Not ambiguous as worded.
